segments.speaker: Julie Showalter
segments.text: I'm Julie Showalter. I grew up on a turkey farm in southwest Missouri. "The night 3,000 turkeys died." The day before the night that 3,000 turkeys died, we moved 13,000 turkeys to the range.

segments.speaker: Julie Showalter
segments.text: This requires some explanation. Turkeys spend their first 16 weeks in a heated brooder house. When they are 16 weeks old, they are put outside to range in fenced enclosures.

segments.speaker: Julie Showalter
segments.text: Daddy decided we would herd them to the range. It looked simple enough. We made a temporary chute of wire fencing that ran from the double-end doors of the brooder house 50 yards to the pen. We would get behind the turkeys in the brooder house, shout, wave old shirts and gunny sacks at them, and they would run out the doors, through the chute, into the pen.

segments.speaker: Julie Showalter
segments.text: And that's the way it worked in the first brooder house. The first turkeys hesitated at the door, walked out cautiously, then moved through the chute and dispersed. The rest followed. It took about an hour. Daddy was pleased. "Let's work straight through," he said. "We'll be done by 10:00."

segments.speaker: Julie Showalter
segments.text: By the time the turkeys have been in a brooder house for 16 weeks, the air is filled with ammonia, feather particles, and dust. The stench is overwhelming. After an hour in the brooder house, your lungs hurt for a day.

segments.speaker: Julie Showalter
segments.text: You can contract disabling lung diseases from working only a week in a poultry house. Tiny barbed pieces of feather dig into the tissue of your lung and never let go. But we didn't know that then.

segments.speaker: Julie Showalter
segments.text: We moved the temporary fence to the doors of the second brooder house. When we threw open the doors at the end of the second house, it was 9:00 in the morning. The sun streamed in the open doors on turkeys that had never seen direct sunlight.

segments.speaker: Julie Showalter
segments.text: The one thing you can count on with turkeys is that you never know how they are going to react. I've seen turkeys clamber against a fence trying to get into a range fire. I've seen them rush toward a screaming child, trying to kill it. And I've seen them run from a screaming child, spooked and terrified.

segments.speaker: Julie Showalter
segments.text: These turkeys didn't want to go into the sun. As we pushed from behind, they compacted. It was like an old adventure movie where the walls are closing in. But there was no wall at the end, only a patch of sunlight which turkeys would not touch.

segments.speaker: Julie Showalter
segments.text: We yelled louder, waved our cloths, kicked at the ones in the rear. Finally, Daddy walked through the solid carpet of turkeys to break the logjam at the front. He stood at the edge of the sunlight, lifting the turkeys three or four at a time with his feet, stirring them with this legs, forcing them into the sun.

segments.speaker: Julie Showalter
segments.text: Suddenly, they broke free. As stubbornly as they had refused to go into the light, they now rushed toward it. They ran in a panic, piling on top of each other, knocking down the temporary fence. By the time Daddy could get the doors closed, at least 1,000 turkeys had escaped and were running free on the farm, onto our neighbor's farm, into the road.

segments.speaker: Julie Showalter
segments.text: We didn't own the turkeys. We raised them for a company that owned the hatchery, the feed mill, the fleet of trucks that delivered and loaded the turkeys, the processing plant. We got a portion of the profits, if there were profits.

segments.speaker: Julie Showalter
segments.text: With 1,000 turkeys gone, there would be no profits on this flock. 16 weeks of Daddy working 14-hour days, of my sisters and me working alongside him any time we weren't in school, all for no pay. And if we weren't paid for this flock, we would have no cash coming in until the next flock was raised.

segments.speaker: Julie Showalter
segments.text: It took us eight hours to round up the escaped turkeys, four of us trying to track down 1,000 birds that had the whole world in which to hide and run from us. The sun beat down, and the air was thick and humid. We stopped once for water, and my sister, Billie, the youngest of us, just 11, vomited from the cold water hitting her stomach after hours of sun, heat, and dehydration.

segments.speaker: Julie Showalter
segments.text: As she lay on the ground, shaking and holding her stomach, I hated her for being the one too sick to continue. But even she was not too sick. We all went on. She got an extra five minutes to rest, but we all went on.

segments.speaker: Julie Showalter
segments.text: You may be asking right now how my father could be so cruel, how he could work young girls like that? Or you may think that I'm exaggerating, that self-pity has magnified our distress. I tell you, this is no exaggeration. And I tell you, my father had no choice. Or that any choice he had was so far in the past that there was no unraveling it. Years later, when we were grown, we caught a glimpse of his guilt, his bitterness over what he had done to us. "I couldn't afford n------," he told my sister Billie. "So I had daughters."

segments.speaker: Julie Showalter
segments.text: At 6 o'clock, we rebuilt the chute. We opened the doors, and the 6,000 remaining turkeys, the sun now low in the sky behind them, walked through to the pen. We cleaned up. We ate supper. And we went to bed. That's the day we had before the night 3,000 turkeys died.

segments.speaker: Julie Showalter
segments.text: At midnight, Mother woke us up. "We have to get to the pen. Daddy needs us." We had been too exhausted to hear the storm. We ran out in the driving rain. Flashes of lightning showed Daddy picking up turkeys and throwing them, one after the other.

segments.speaker: Julie Showalter
segments.text: When people learn I grew up on a turkey farm, they invariably ask, "Is it true? Are they really so stupid that they open their mouths in the rain, look up at the sky, and drown?" The answer is yes, some of them do that. They are that stupid. But that's not how 3,000 die in one night.

segments.speaker: Julie Showalter
segments.text: They die because they are scared, and they huddle together in their fear. They climb on top of each other, trying to get close, to find protection in the mass of bodies. And they suffocate.

segments.speaker: Julie Showalter
segments.text: We called it piling. It wasn't unusual for a loud noise to cause a pile in the brooder house. If there wasn't someone to pull them off each other, 50 could die because someone slammed a door.

segments.speaker: Julie Showalter
segments.text: But this was worse than any pile we'd seen, turkeys who'd never spent a night outdoors panicked by thunder, lightning, and rain in sheets. All we could do is pull them out of the pile and throw them away from it. They would run back, still seeking the comfort of the group.

segments.speaker: Julie Showalter
segments.text: After a while standing in mud, grabbing soaked turkeys, throwing them, grabbing more, you don't know if the ones you are throwing are dead or alive. You don't care. Maybe we saved some.

segments.speaker: Julie Showalter
segments.text: The next day, the sky was cloudless, and the sun bore down on us again. We picked up dead turkeys, throwing them onto the back of a flatbed truck. Daddy drove the truck into a field far from the house. He poured gasoline on them and struck a match. They burned for days.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Well, Julie Showalter lives in Burr Ridge, Illinois, and says that she still does eat turkey. Well, twice a year, she eats it. And this is the special Poultry Slam edition of Your Radio Playhouse, coming to you from WBEZ in Chicago. Stay with us, won't you?

segments.speaker: Luis Rodriguez
segments.text: This is Luis Rodriguez. And I'm going to read my poem, "The Rooster Who Thought it Was a Dog." Echo Park mornings came on the wings of a rooster's gnawing squawk. This noise, unfortunately, also brought in the afternoon, evenings, and most hours of the day. The rooster had no sense of time, nor any desire to commit to one. He'd cock-a-doodle whenever he had the notion.

segments.speaker: Luis Rodriguez
segments.text: For late sleepers, day sleepers, or your plain, ordinary, run of the mill night sleepers, annoyance had this rooster's beak. It was enough to drive one crazy. Often, I open my back window that faced the alley just across from the backyard where the rooster made his home. "Shut up, or I'll blow your stinking brains out," I'd yell. Great communication technique.

segments.speaker: Luis Rodriguez
segments.text: It worked on the brats next door, but the rooster never flinched. With calm aplomb, it continued to squawk. For one thing, the rooster never gave out a bona fide cock-a-doodle. It sort of shouted it out.

segments.speaker: Luis Rodriguez
segments.text: It happened that the rooster lived with three dogs, a German Shepherd and two mutts. The dogs barked through their existence. They barked at everything in sight. I finally concluded that rooster thought it was a dog. Somehow, I didn't mind the dogs barking. But when a rooster barks, that's murder.

segments.speaker: Luis Rodriguez
segments.text: In fact, I often saw it running alongside the dogs as they raced across the dirt yard, barking at passing cars or people. If the dogs went left, the rooster went left. They'd go right, and dang if that rooster didn't go right as well. Now I don't know if this is a regular condition for roosters.

segments.speaker: Luis Rodriguez
segments.text: I thought I had a story for the Weekly World News. I could see it now. "The Rooster Who Thinks it's a Dog." Who knows what rooster dementia we had here? And whether the rooster chased cats up trees or pissed on fire hydrants, this wasn't clear.

segments.speaker: Luis Rodriguez
segments.text: But once I grasped the heart of the matter, I began to see the rooster in another light. I felt sorry for this fowl with an identity problem. And I wondered how it must react when its owners threw chicken bones to the dogs. Would it nibble on the remains of its favorite hen? I shuddered at the thought.

segments.speaker: Luis Rodriguez
segments.text: Yet despite the revelation of the rooster's bark, the problem of sleep didn't end. Then one day, a new neighbor, a young lady, who often drank herself to bliss, got a gun and blew the rooster away. She became somewhat of a local hero.

segments.speaker: Luis Rodriguez
segments.text: I must say, though, it was an unfitting end for the bird. But I suppose one can tolerate barking dogs. But barking roosters? That's another matter altogether.

segments.speaker: David Sedaris
segments.text: July 19, 1992. This afternoon, at the 26th Street Flea Market, I had one of those experiences that remind me why I shop in the first place. Not shop like grocery shop, but step out into the world searching for that one thing I cannot name.

segments.speaker: David Sedaris
segments.text: I pass the usual objects, the grinning mammies offering themselves up as salt and pepper shakers, the coffee table made from dice, another head carved from a coconut. "That's collectible," the dealers say, referring to an ashtray in the shape of a doll-sized toilet bowl. Collectible to who?

segments.speaker: David Sedaris
segments.text: Last weekend at the flea market, I saw this thing, a taxidermied turkey's head attached to its own foot. This turkey was equipped with that length of flesh that spills from the top of its beak and fell to its neck. Stiff red hair stood out from the head and shoulders, and the claws were really sharp. You'd think that something armed like that might be able to protect itself.

segments.speaker: David Sedaris
segments.text: I pictured its maker standing by a chopping block saying, "I know. I'll take the turkey's head and attach it to the foot." Why would you do that? Or more importantly, what sort of life would you lead that might enable you to make this connection?

segments.speaker: David Sedaris
segments.text: I was hypnotized by this object and asked the price as if I were under a spell. "$45," the dealer said. My tongue was dry from hanging in the open air, and I tried to fit it back into my mouth. "All right," she said, "$35. $30." But she could have gone up. "All right. $85. $120. $370."

segments.speaker: David Sedaris
segments.text: I had no choice but to follow wherever she led me. I handed over my wallet in a trance, just gave it to her, thinking she could take the whole thing, the cash, blank checks, library card, whatever. Take it all.

segments.speaker: David Sedaris
segments.text: I stared into the face of this taxidermied turkey's head, and nothing else mattered. Tomorrow, what's that? Yesterday doesn't count. My life began the moment I could call this thing my own.

segments.speaker: David Sedaris
segments.text: On the way home I felt giddy and confident that I could approach anyone at all and say, "I'll give you one hundred-- no, $500,000 if you can guess what I've got in this paper sack." And I swear that not one of them could have come up with the right answer. I walked home 30 blocks, looking everyone square in the eye and thinking, "Sucker."

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Well, David Sedaris is the author of Barrel Fever, often heard on NPR's Morning Edition.

segments.text: That's my Chicken Mask. The beak and, you know, the feathers.

segments.speaker: Dupont Chopper
segments.text: Uh-huh. Well, don't look at small children or animals. Anyway, that's the health story. But I don't think you have to alter your lifestyle, unless you are a crimefighting superhero of some kind.

segments.speaker: Dupont Chopper
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Dupont Chopper
segments.text: Want to buy one of my tapes?

segments.speaker: Benton Harbor
segments.text: 12:00 noon. I return to the Chicken Cave. And there, in the chicken mirror-- augh!-- I see something horrible. No, not my ugly face, my own mortality. I ask myself why it never stared me in the face before. After all, I've been fighting crime and/or evil for over 30 years, pursuing it down streets and allies and sewers and other picturesque places. And my mortality never came up even once.

segments.speaker: Benton Harbor
segments.text: 1:40 PM. I go see the police commissioner and share with him the doctor's diagnosis. After all, he is my closest friend. And if I can't tell him the bad news, who can I tell? So I give him a new coloring book I bought for him and tell him my sad news. And he says--

segments.speaker: Police Commissioner
segments.text: Ha, ha. This looks like a real neat coloring book.

segments.speaker: Benton Harbor
segments.text: So what do you think commissioner?

segments.speaker: Police Commissioner
segments.text: About what?

segments.speaker: Benton Harbor
segments.text: What I just shared with you.

segments.speaker: Police Commissioner
segments.text: Oh. It's a real neat coloring book.

segments.speaker: Benton Harbor
segments.text: About the diagnosis and the need to alter my lifestyle.

segments.speaker: Police Commissioner
segments.text: Oh. Well, that would mean that you'd have to-- and of course one can't even be sure that that, you know. So anyway, that's how I see it.

segments.speaker: Dupont Chopper
segments.text: OK. Thanks, commissioner.

segments.speaker: Police Commissioner
segments.text: Anytime, winged warrior. After all, what are friends for? And may I ask you a question?

segments.speaker: Benton Harbor
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Police Commissioner
segments.text: If I make the sky blue in this picture and the mountains brown, do you think the rocks should be chartreuse?

segments.speaker: Benton Harbor
segments.text: Perfect.

segments.speaker: Benton Harbor
segments.text: 4:00 PM. I go to the local office of the Grace Hill Ferguson Employment Agency and Screen Door Company.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: OK, when you say something more sed-ren-tarry, what do you mean?

segments.speaker: Benton Harbor
segments.text: Sedentary. You know, things where I can seden-- sit.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Oh, OK. What kind of previous work experience do you have?

segments.speaker: Benton Harbor
segments.text: Basically fighting crime and/or evil.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: And what special equipment, office or otherwise, are you experienced in using?

segments.speaker: Benton Harbor
segments.text: Geshtukna ray gun.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Could you spell that?

segments.speaker: Benton Harbor
segments.text: G-E-S-H-T-U-K-A-N-A. And I also worked a Chicken Dissolver and a Chicken Modulator and a can opener.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: OK. Do you know Windows 95?

segments.speaker: Benton Harbor
segments.text: Look, what light job openings are on your list there? Just look.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Heavy cable puller, refrigerator and piano mover, cement hailer--

segments.speaker: Benton Harbor
segments.text: Hauler.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: OK. Big tree planter! Circus tent--

segments.speaker: Benton Harbor
segments.text: Miss?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: What?

segments.speaker: Benton Harbor
segments.text: Not holler. Those are all active and heavy things. Anything light I could do?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Yes, a negligee model in a delicatessen.

segments.speaker: Benton Harbor
segments.text: I don't--

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Oh, well scratch that, then. Requires previous experience. Oh, here's something really perfect.

segments.speaker: Benton Harbor
segments.text: What's that?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: A napkin-folder in a nouveau Italian-Chinese restaurant specializing in pizza and light salads. Takeout available. Mmm, I'm hungry.

segments.speaker: Benton Harbor
segments.text: Wednesday morning, 9:30 AM. My Chicken Alarm goes off a half hour late for my geriatric counseling appointment. Tire still flat. So I take the convenient number 18 bus. And that leaves me off only 28 blocks from the counselor's office.

segments.speaker: Counselor
segments.text: I have one word of advice, Mister. Get out.

segments.speaker: Benton Harbor
segments.text: Excuse me?

segments.speaker: Counselor
segments.text: Get out.

segments.speaker: Benton Harbor
segments.text: OK, I'm a few minutes late.

segments.speaker: Counselor
segments.text: What? You're 30 years too late. Get out.

segments.speaker: Benton Harbor
segments.text: Oh, you mean get out, not get out.

segments.speaker: Counselor
segments.text: May I suggest a small, desert, superhero retirement community.

segments.speaker: Benton Harbor
segments.text: Ooh.

segments.speaker: Counselor
segments.text: You play golf?

segments.speaker: Benton Harbor
segments.text: Not real good, no.

segments.speaker: Counselor
segments.text: Good, you'll fit right in. Neither does Fishwoman or that Flying Newt. I sent them there. They love it.

segments.speaker: Benton Harbor
segments.text: Fishwoman?

segments.speaker: Counselor
segments.text: Yeah. Little scaly, nice personality.

segments.speaker: Benton Harbor
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Counselor
segments.text: Want to buy one of my tapes?

segments.speaker: Benton Harbor
segments.text: 2:00 AM, next morning. I can't sleep, and I sip warm milk in the Chicken Cave. What to do? I'm on the horns of a dilemma. Heavy concrete hauler? Fold napkins in nouveau Italian-Chinese restaurant specializing in pizza and light salads? Or challenge the fates?

segments.speaker: Benton Harbor
segments.text: 8:00 AM. I stand on the roof of Midland City's tallest skyscraper, four dizzy stories high. I hurl a challenge to the fates. This is the winged warrior, fates. I shall go on fighting crime and/or evil. I don't care that my bad cholesterol is bad, that--

segments.speaker: Benton Harbor
segments.text: Suddenly, a black cloud forms swiftly in the sky, and I hear--

segments.speaker: Frank The Fate
segments.text: OK, do what you want. We'll try to be there for you. But watch the fatty foods, the cookies, the ice cream, and good luck to you.

segments.speaker: Benton Harbor
segments.text: Who is that?

segments.speaker: Frank The Fate
segments.text: One of the fates.

segments.speaker: Benton Harbor
segments.text: Which one?

segments.speaker: Frank The Fate
segments.text: Frank. Phyllis, Fran and Fred are in Las Vegas. God bless them, they should only win and be well.

segments.speaker: Benton Harbor
segments.text: OK. Well, fine. I'll just carry on, then.

segments.speaker: Frank The Fate
segments.text: OK. Listen, could you change that mask you're wearing now? It's very ugly and could scare kids and small animals. Thank you very much.

segments.speaker: Benton Harbor
segments.text: Right.

segments.speaker: Benton Harbor
segments.text: And at that moment, I knew fate was blind, and I, the famous fowl, would have the last laugh. For you see, I wasn't wearing a mask.

segments.speaker: Benton Harbor
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Chickenman Announcer
segments.text: Well, what has the winged warrior gotten himself into here? Can he actually stop time by challenging the fates? And is it Frank Fate he's talking to or Georgie Jessel? And another thing, doesn't that nouveau Italian-Chinese restaurant sound super-trendy? Be listening tomorrow for another exciting episode in the life of the most fantastic crimefighter the world has ever known.

segments.speaker: Chickenman
segments.text: Bock bock bock bock!

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Chickenman.

segments.speaker: Women
segments.text: He's everywhere, he's everywhere!

segments.speaker: Danielle
segments.text: I just want a real person who's like Duki, probably. I want to go marry some guy who's like Duki.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And how's that search going?

segments.speaker: Danielle
segments.text: Not well.

segments.text: I'm Ira Glass. See you next week, same chicken time, same chicken channel. Same brave little radio station.

segments.speaker: Danielle
segments.text: Ira?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Hmm?

segments.speaker: Danielle
segments.text: Don't make me sound like an idiot, OK?
